endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: To avoid conflict of interest, it is important that the validator of the solution is not also the developer of the solution.

evidence.title: Is the generalizability of a developed artificial intelligence algorithm for COVID-19 on chest CT sufficient for clinical use? Results from the International Consortium for COVID-19 Imaging AI (ICOVAI)
evidence.outcome: Independent external validation versus internal testing by developers
evidence.effect: Independent validation revealed significantly lower performance (kappa 0.62 vs 0.78; opacity DSC 0.59 vs 0.76), showing that internal results overstated performance.
evidence.quote: The study demonstrates the importance of independent external validation of AI models.

evidence.title: Evaluating AI diagnostic accuracy in approximal dental caries detection on bitewing radiographs
evidence.outcome: Independent validation of a commercial AI tool by a party other than developer
evidence.effect: Independent validation of Diagnocat on bitewing radiographs found moderate sensitivity (73.1%) and low PPV (64.7%), so performance claims were tempered.
evidence.quote: This study offers an independent validation of Diagnocat™ using bitewing radiographs.

commentary.bottom_line: Two retrospective imaging studies suggest that validation by a party independent of the developer may produce lower performance estimates than developer-reported results, which fits the concern that developer testing overstates accuracy. Neither study tested a governance committee requirement or measured patient outcomes, so certainty is very low.

perspectives.view: Both studies are level 4 retrospective replays in offline settings. In the European CT study, independent validation gave a kappa of 0.62 against 0.78 from developer testing, and an opacity DSC of 0.59 against 0.76. The Cyprus dental study reported 73.1% sensitivity and 64.7% PPV without a direct developer comparator. Indirectness and small samples lower certainty to very low.

The gap between internal and independent results in the CT study suggests that a tool approved on developer figures may perform worse than expected. A PPV of 64.7% in the dental study implies that about one in three positive flags may be false, which could prompt unneeded treatment. Neither study followed errors through to patient harm.

Both validations used archived images outside live workflows. They show what independent testing can detect, but they do not show how a governance committee would staff, schedule, or enforce it. Neither study reports the time, expertise, or data access the independent validators needed, so the burden of routine adoption remains unmeasured.

Neither study reported patient insurance, income, language, or literacy. The samples came from hospitals in the Netherlands, Belgium, and Italy and from a dental setting in Cyprus. Independent validation might expose larger performance gaps in groups underrepresented in developer data, but these studies did not examine that question.

commentary.research_gap: No study has compared governance processes that require an independent validator with processes that accept developer validation, and none has measured effects on deployment decisions, post-deployment error rates, patient outcomes, or validation cost. The existing tests cover two imaging tools in European settings. Prospective studies of non-imaging tools in U.S. health systems, including safety-net hospitals, would address the main gaps.
commentary.underserved_note: Neither study reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The findings therefore offer no direct information on whether independent validation detects performance shortfalls that affect these groups, and health systems serving them cannot assume the reported discrepancies apply to their patients.
